How do I tell my daughter the chip on her dresser doesn't mean what it meant last week? I keep his reading glasses on the nightstand, folded, waiting. Her voicemail said call anytime, so I did, at 3 a.m., shaking, and she picked up like it was noon. I laughed at something on TV tonight and then sat very still, ashamed, then not ashamed, then just tired. My sponsor answered on the second ring, and the first thing she said was that she was glad I called. The app asked if I was sure before resetting my counter to zero, and I sat with my thumb hovering for a long time. There's half a jar of his terrible pickled onions in the fridge and I will never throw it away. Everyone at the eight o'clock group already knew before I opened my mouth; small rooms carry news fast. Telling my teenage son was harder than the detox ever was, because he remembered the last time. Day two, and the coffee tastes the way it did in the first ninety, bitter and necessary and endless. Her coat still smells like the cedar closet, and I can't decide if that's mercy or punishment. Slept maybe two hours; the rest was ceiling-staring and replaying the last voicemail until the words stopped meaning anything. What I keep replaying is the moment in the parking lot when I still could have driven home. Maybe the slip doesn't erase the three years; maybe it just proves I can't ever coast on them. Our bed is an acreage of cold cotton now, and I keep to one edge like a guest. At the podium I couldn't get past my name for a while, and nobody rushed me. Four months out and I still reach for my phone every Sunday at six. Walking back into the Thursday meeting felt like standing under fluorescent lights with my whole year written on my face. Eleven hundred and four days, gone in one Tuesday afternoon I still can't fully explain to myself. Sunday dinners are back to short answers and long silences, and I earned every minute of them.
